#6802. The GTA Files: My Long-Lost Interview With the Brothers Who Founded Rockstar

“You can’t fuck with Keith Richards.” That’s what Sam Houser told me when I asked the inspiration for his company name, Rockstar Games. “I’m a huge fan of the classic golden era of rock stars—both the music, but also the life,” he went on. “You can't argue with Keith Moon riding in a Rolls Royce with a blowup doll hanging out the back and a woman in there screaming, ‘I'm being raped.’ The guy is the original punk rocker. And if we can bring a fraction of that to games, then we’re doing something.”

It was October 2002, just a few weeks before the release of their latest blockbuster, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. I’d come to their glossy loft in Soho, Manhattan to interview the elusive 30-year-old Houser and Rockstar co-founders, his younger brother Dan Houser and managing director Terry Donovan, for Rolling Stone. It would be one of their first, last and only in-depth sit-downs together before they decided that the world’s most successful and controversial video game required little explanation from them at all.

I continued reporting on them and their games during the raucous and turbulent years to follow: hitting over $10 billion in sales, getting compared to Balzac and Dickens in Time magazine, being sued (unsuccessfully) for causing real-life violence. As I investigated in my book Jacked: The Outlaw Story of Grand Theft Auto, they also triggered what remains the most outrageous and cinematic scandal ever to hit the industry: the discovery of a hidden sex scene in 2005’s GTA San Andreas that would inspire attempts to legislate and ban the game. As Hilary Clinton said at the time, “The disturbing material in Grand Theft Auto and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children and it’s making the difficult job of being a parent even harder.”

With the gamer generation now grown up and in power, the Reefer Madness panic around GTA has finally given way to something more important: this little game out of Scotland has become the most successful and influential entertainment product of all time. Today, Rockstar returns to Vice City with the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. More than a decade in the making, with a budget Rockstar has never disclosed but analysts put between $1 billion and $2 billion, the game follows Jason Duval, an ex-soldier, and Lucia Caminos, who phones him from prison, as they’re pulled into a criminal conspiracy across a send-up of Miami. Its first trailer has been viewed more than 300 million times on YouTube, and footage premiering on Netflix nearly crashed the streamer’s servers. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, expects record revenue of $8.1 billion this fiscal year.

For longtime fans, GTA 6 marks something more personal: the first game in the franchise since the original band behind it broke up. Following the departure of Donovan and other central figures, Dan Houser exited Rockstar in 2020, leaving his big brother Sam as the last founder still there. With Sam remaining notoriously quiet about the new game, I went digging through my old tapes and found my long-lost interview with gaming’s original punk rockers. During our two-hour talk, the young co-founders were brash, unrepentant, and championing a lifetime of obsessions, as Sam put it. “I wasn’t just obsessed about games,” he told me, “we were obsessed about everything—obsessive about music, obsessive about film, obsessive about fashion.”

GTA 6 shows that the obsession never left him. Here in this exclusive excerpt from my interview, the Rockstars share how it all started.

Sam Houser: We nearly had a fist fight last week. We have one argument a year.

Sam Houser: That was an old arcade game called Mr. Do! It used to be in like, a bodega, a corner store. You go in there and buy a cigarette for seven P. And you get a couple of games of Mr. Do!. But the games that really got me hooked was when I got into the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. It was very British: a weird little computer with rubber keys, and it was the games that came out then. I was obsessive about everything, really. We had every significant game on every game system going.

Dan Houser: They thought it was interesting. Sam was probably more into games throughout the time. I would come in and out from being interested in them, or being forced to play them. There was physical violence.

Sam Houser: I would beat him into playing.

Terry Donovan: I think for me, there was a period of arcade games: Defender, Track and Field, Tron, Pole Position. So that was that was like the golden age. You would you stand there and if a bloke lasted two hours on 10p on Defender, you thought he was it. If you grew up in the '70s, you probably wanted to be a guitarist. If you were in the '80s, you probably wanted to be a DJ. The things you grow up wanting now, you probably want to be a video game designer.

Sam Houser: Absolutely. That’s one of the essential things, for me, in games. Look at the games we do now. The game that really coined that in the early days, particularly for me, was this game Elite. You were a space smuggler, and it was just very simple graphics—black screen with just white lights on it. And you flew around space, interacting with other spaceships and other colonies and other planets and so on.

Dan Houser: It's like reading any kind of book when you're a kid or anything that makes you feel like you're not in the real world.

Sam Houser: What was interesting about GTA 1 was that graphically it was top down. It wasn't as sharp or appealing as things that were popular at the time, like Tomb Raider and all these other games that were coming out. You were put into the world, and you were given choices. It was a very sort of non-linear experience. Because it showed all these people out there that wanted this kind of experience that were prepared to forego the graphical gratification you got at the Tomb Raider—you know, that girl with the nice breasts. Suddenly you were playing in 2D and it was top down. It was utterly compelling.

I thought the subject matter was a really appealing hook. We felt that the sort of the fantasy sci-fi, fantasy, you know, Dungeons & Dragons, and here's my sword and there's that orc. We didn't feel that the mass market was that into that stuff. We wanted to make things that felt a little bit more relevant to people like ourselves. The reason it sold is it was incredibly fun to play. It was originally called Race n' Chase. Kind of catchy name. In the UK, the game was in the House of Parliament, and it got a massive share of media attention. It was on BBC News five times in one day. Like, oh my God!

Terry Donovan: It was one first piece of entertainment that was sort of unashamed antihero. There's no twist at the end where he turns out to be a good guy.

Dan Houser: Freedom was the thing that appealed. Because as free as games like Defender and Scramble were for us, 10 years on, they felt restrictive. I don't consider myself a master gamer. I play every game. I'm good at them. But I think that we try and make games that can be played by normal folk as well as hardcore too. And the problem with some of those other games is when you hit a point that's frustrating, you can't get past it. But in Grand Theft Auto, any of them, when you hit a point that's tough, you just go and do something else. And then while you're doing the other thing, you're thinking about this other thing that you've been stuck on, and then you come back to it and crack it. I think that's fucking great.

Sam Houser: I came out here and did a very energetic pitch where I must have sweated through three layers of clothing in my kind of insanely sweaty way, and everyone in the office was like, "Who the fuck is that guy?"

Sam Houser: They just didn't want it. Business is so like, “What's that person doing? We must copy that.” Everybody else was doing 3D platform games and 3D sports games, all these shooters.

Sam Houser: I first came here in my 18th birthday. It my 18th birthday present or whatever to just go and buy leather hip-hop puffers and Air Jordan Mark V's. From that moment I was chronically in love with the place. The idea that I would end up here making games where games is traditionally a West Coast thing, to me it's just like… in some ways I feel it was meant to be. We were kind of enlisted to sort of build that.

Sam Houser: The mission was basically to bring our attitude, to try and make games that felt more relevant to the audience that was playing.

Dan Houser: It’s more modern, more accessible, gameplay over graphics, but with a slightly anarchic, edgy fantasy—a fantasy you would have walking down the street rather than from reading Dungeons & Dragons. It’s a fantasy where you're a street racer rather than a wizard.

Terry Donovan: [to Sam] How much did you want a Def Jam baseball jacket?

Sam Houser: More than anything in the world. They had this attitude: “Here's where we from. Here's what we do. If you don't like us, fuck you. Everything we touch is somehow made more magical.” A guy like Rick Rubin is such a fucking hero, because you go from doing the hip-hop that he pioneered to doing Slayer, to doing The Cult.

Terry Donovan: It was a first-floor apartment on Water Street, in the South Street Seaport, and it had glass on the front. There was no fucking light in it.

Sam Houser: There was about 20 people. By the time I was in there, there was about seven people living in there. That whole teenager-in-the-bedroom-with-the-bottle-top-specs thing comes around the games industry like a fucking albatross. This wasn't the kind of lonely nine-year-old or 12-year-old kid, or the one who's going to end up exposing himself to schoolgirl doing this.

Terry Donovan: The lines are our decision of what's funny and what's tasteful. What isn't relevant to what a lot of what other people think. If you think it's funny, you put it in your machine, if you don't think it's funny, you don't. By the time you've reduced Grand Theft Auto on national television to a 30-second soundbite, it's a game with a hooker in it, and that's offensive to the very, very maximum. That's the thing—you realize that [gamers] aren't all 10 years old. There isn't some overriding social responsibility to have a redeeming social value. Our responsibility is to provide a toolkit with which young adults can entertain themselves.

Sam Houser: When you do something wrong in the game, the police come and get you. You don't just run around on a rampage and carry on. You commit crimes, the police are on you. You commit more, they're on you more. You commit more, the FBI will turn up, the SWAT will turn up, and then the Army turns up. When you play the missions, you're only you're only doing bad things to bad people. You're whacking other gangsters.

Sam Houser: When I play it for fun, I tend to just drive around and look at cool things and drive in as cinematic a way as possible— sort of like I’m a stifled film director. And I’m carrying out my own little stories in my own head, listening the music. I mean, gosh, I am 30 years old. It's sort of tragic, isn't it? I just sort of go off in my own world.

Sam Houser: Oh, well, Scarface, Miami Vice. At the end of GTA III, we took our whole team out to Miami. We're all out there. This is we live and breathe this place, learn this place. For research, we were staying in a very average hotel on Ocean Drive. You know, it was 30 Scottish guys walking around with cameras in the day. The second half of the week, everyone got insanely burned.

Dan Houser: Vice City is not quite Miami. It's Miami through the Grand Theft Auto lens. On the other hand, you don't want to offend the nerds because you've not put the right number of bridges in, or things are a little bit different. You know, we're so anal that we don't want to offend other anal people. For example, with the radio commercials, me and the other guy, one of the other guys who just then with me would sit for hours and listen to '80s radio commercials. We got we ring up advertising agencies and say, ‘send us all your best best '80s radio and TV commercials.’

Sam Houser: We're trying to do a satire about the 80s.

Sam Houser: We cast them ourselves. Contact their agents ourselves. Tommy Vercetti is played by Ray Liotta, interacting with Lance Vance, Philip Michael Thomas, [Ricardo] Tubbs from Miami Vice. The two of them together, they have these really entertaining moments.

Dan Houser: Her character is a porn star. She was really sweet, though. She was really lovely. She turned up with her husband and her mother and father, and I'm particularly very English in these situations, so I'm feeling slightly… I'm going, "Oh, hello, Jenna. Could you sound like you're excited?" And she's looking at me more and more obliquely and says "Well, how would it be if I sound like I was having sex?" And I'm like, “Well, that'd be actually perfect.”

Sam Houser: My favorite thing is probably the overall look. I think the thing that we set up so much stuff on was, get me neon. We've got to have neon!

Dan Houser: You can do everything you can do in a film and more. It's all the bits that go in between the equivalent plots of about five films. But it's a different experience compared to a film.

Sam Houser: Almost by definition, no. Apart from choose-your-own-adventure books. You feel like, “Hey, [I have] my little piece of digital real estate, and there's my car and everything. I own this little space.” It's just some numbers and ones and all this code. When the machine's on and it's going, it's there, it's real.

Terry Donovan: There's no point being edgy if your game's a shit.

Sam Houser: At the end of the day, there's enough people in the country that would like to see us thrown out and/or locked up for doing what we do. Look at the trouble we got in for the prostitute thing. You'd be amazed how conservative people are.

#6801. Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Despite Robert Pattinson’s big-screen career and Suki Waterhouse’s supermodel status, the public doesn’t know much about their relationship. Both of these Brits prefer to keep their private lives out of the public sphere. As their romance continues past the five-year mark and the couple settles into parenthood, here’s a rundown of their secretive story.

Pattinson and Waterhouse were first linked on July 30 when E! obtained photos of the pair kissing in the streets of London. Per the outlet’s report, the two saw a 9 P.M. showing of Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again at Electric Cinema in Notting Hill. They then walked across the street for drinks at SoHo House until 1 A.M.An eyewitness said the couple was open with their affection. “Along the way, they were very close and cuddled and kissed many times,” the source told E! News. “Robert was very affectionate to her and had his arm around her the whole way and Suki reciprocated by holding his hand and kissing it. They were very loved up and close. Robert stroked Suki’s hair and gave her another loving kiss.”

An E! source said the pair was only “casually dating.” Since Pattinson had only recently ended a three-year relationship, “he isn’t looking for anything serious right now.”

The insider did express that the two “are definitely into each other” and are dating while Pattinson is in London filming The King. “Rob likes to have fun when he has breaks in-between filming and him and Suki have a great time together,” the source added.

LaineyGossip disputed breakup rumors that surfaced at the time, sharing that Pattinson had FaceTimed Waterhouse walking home from a London pub in August. Per the outlet’s report, the couple was spotted at Miguel’s concert in Los Angeles.

They each also attended the Toronto International Film Festival for their own projects that month. Pattinson was promoting High Life while Waterhouse walked the carpet for Assassination Nation.

The couple was photographed exiting London club Chiltern Firehouse at 2:15 A.M., seemingly confirming they were still together.

Photos surfaced of the couple leaving a Christmas party on London’s Regent Street. Waterhouse and Pattinson stayed at the party until the early morning hours.

Waterhouse and Pattinson spent her 27th birthday together, photographed leaving her party. A couple weeks later, People ran photos of them holding hands after a run in London.

Pattinson made his first public comments about his relationship with Waterhouse.

The Sunday Times asked Pattinson about Waterhouse, and he responded by asking, “Do I have to [talk about her]?” Then he went into more detail about why he’s so private about his personal life:

“If you let people in, it devalues what love is. If a stranger on the street asked you about your relationship, you’d think it extremely rude. If you put up a wall it ends up better. I can’t understand how someone can walk down the street holding hands, and it’s the same as when I do it and a hundred people are taking your photo. The line between when you’re performing and when you’re not will eventually get washed away, and you’ll go completely mad.”

However, he did tell the outlet that breakups with Kristen Stewart and FKA Twigs didn’t disillusion him to romance with a celebrity. “They were pretty long relationships, not like three months.”

When it came time for Pattinson’s 33rd birthday, he and Waterhouse were photographed at Chateau Marmont. Pattinson’s friend Tom Sturridge was also in attendance for the celebrations, per People.

During a June interview with Grazia, the reporter noted that Waterhouse FaceTimed Pattinson during a photo shoot break.

E! published a picture of Pattinson and Waterhouse strolling through London as they marked one year of dating.

In early September, photographer Sofia Malamute shared a photo of the couple cuddled together, captioned, “Ibiza, 2019.”

After several months of staying out of the public eye, Waterhouse and Pattinson confirmed their relationship was still going strong. The pair was seen leaving Waterhouse’s 27th birthday party in London on January 12, per LaineyGossip.

They celebrated her birthday at London’s Casa Cruz, and attendees included Liv Tyler, Georgia May Jagger, Cara Delevingne, and Ashley Benson.

Pattinson essentially confirmed that he was quarantining with Waterhouse during an interview for GQ’s June cover. According to the article, Pattinson had been sequestered “with his girlfriend” in the London apartment “the Batman folks rented for him” while production on the film was paused.

The couple signaled they were still going strong, two years into their relationship, with a pair of public outings. On July 21, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed walking arm-in-arm around London’s Notting Hill.

A source spoke to E! about the sighting, telling the outlet, “They weren’t recognized by anyone and they seemed to be in their own little world as they took a long stroll around the village chatting intently, pointing at properties and laughing together before they arrived at the club. They held hands the whole time or were linking arms and looked very happy.”

The following day, People published another photo of the couple on a walk. An insider told the outlet, “They are very loved-up,” adding, “they haven’t been together that long. But everything seems on the fast track. They are always laughing and smiling at each other.”

The pair’s most PDA-filled photo yet arrived about 12 days after Pattinson was reported to have tested positive for COVID-19, per CBS News. Although the studio never confirmed that report, production on The Batman was “temporarily paused.” It resumed in September, days after Pattinson and Waterhouse’s outing. In the photo, the couple sat on a London park bench with coffees, kissing while their masks were pulled down to their chins.

Pattinson’s recovery apparently only strengthened his relationship. A source told E! that “Rob and Suki have definitely discussed getting engaged but are in no rush. Suki is not pressuring him, and they are both very committed to each other.”

The insider confirmed the couple’s romance is “stronger than ever” after quarantine. “They love being low-key together and have very similar interests,” the source added. “They are truly inseparable and in love.”

Shortly after E! reported the two had discussed getting engaged, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed out with Pattinson’s parents in London. The two walked side-by-side behind Pattinson’s mom and dad on November 23. They opted not to show any PDA in front of them or the photographers who captured this outing.

After months out of the limelight, Waterhouse made headlines when she posted a selfie of herself on April 15. Eagle-eyed fans noticed that a photo of her kissing Pattinson was visible in the background.

On April 19, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed out in London for the first time in 2021. The two held hands while walking in Notting Hill. Both dressed casually, wearing shorts and hoodies. It served as a rare public signal that a year into quarantine, the couple’s relationship remained strong.

Waterhouse called out the HBO Max Gossip Girl reboot for making a joke at her expense. The joke in question: Teen public relations whiz Luna (Zión Moreno) is trying to talk Zoya (Whitney Peak) into stepping up her influencer game. She says, “When are you going to get it? As far as the press is concerned, he’s R-Patz, and you’re Suki Nobody.”

In a now-deleted series of tweets, Waterhouse responded with the following: “Another day to be reminded that women can also be the patriarchy. Seeing critiques of patriarchy and sexism, then I get name-checked as somebody’s ‘nobody’ girlfriend,” per Glamour.

Some fans compared Waterhouse’s response to Taylor Swift’s tweet about Netflix’s Ginny & Georgia’s joke about her.

“Hey Ginny & Georgia, 2010 called and it wants its lazy, deeply sexist joke back. How about we stop degrading hard working women by defining this horse shit as FuNnY,” she wrote. “Also, @netflix after Miss Americana this outfit doesn’t look cute on you Happy Women’s History Month I guess.”

A source gave E! a rare and brief update on how Waterhouse and Pattinson were doing three years into dating: great, naturally.

“They are very solid in their relationship,” the source said. During the rare public appearances they do together, they’re “always just totally joined at the hip. You can tell he’s completely in love with her,” the source said.

Ahead of the holidays, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed on December 8 holding hands in New York City on a winter day date. Pattinson wore a monochrome blue look consisting of a hooded puffer jacket with matching blue pants. Waterhouse chose earth tones, stepping out in a brown Carhartt hat, rose-colored wool coat, and a black Dior cashmere shawl. It was their first time being photographed out together in months.

Pattinson opened up a little about his life with Waterhouse in two interviews during his The Batman press tour.

To GQ, he spoke about her impact on his decision-making—and how she trolled him by talking with a repairman at their place about DC Comics.

Pattinson said Waterhouse was the reason why he changed the location for his GQ interview from the London Zoo to Holland Park. “I was talking to my girlfriend last night and she was, like, ‘You know, people don’t really like zoos.…’” he said. “I’d been thinking about a metaphorical thing. But then I was thinking that’s very wrong, a sad bear walking in circles. I just can’t help it. I’ll do it for every single element, every decision, in my life. What is the worst-case scenario for this decision?”

And with the repairman for their place’s boiler, “The guy came around the other day, and he just randomly started talking about what a DC [Comics] fan he is. And I’m sitting there facing the other direction, and my girlfriend just keeps continuing the conversation with him. And I’m looking at her like: Shut the fuck up!” He laughed. “Why are you doing this to me? She was very entertaining. Just talking to an obsessive fan.”

Pattinson later talked on Jimmy Kimmel Live! about Waterhouse’s emotional reaction watching The Batman and how it made him more terrified of its release. “It was really her reaction that kind of changed the entire thing because I’m pretty sure she’s not normally into watching superhero movies,” he said, via Entertainment Tonight. “And just seeing that it was capturing her attention the entire time and then she held my hand and touched it [to her face] and I could feel a little tear. And I was like, ‘No way!’”

On Friday, May 6, the couple was spotted in Los Angeles after Waterhouse’s show at The Echo. She was touring to promote her new album, I Can’t Let Go. Pattinson was in a baseball cap and mask to keep a low profile. He was wearing a black jacket, gray T-shirt, and a pair of jeans with sneakers. His girlfriend was in jeans and a colorful long-sleeve shirt over a sparkling top. She had on a pair of black boots with a chunky heel.

They walked down the street as Waterhouse spoke into her phone, and Pattinson threw a casual arm around her waist. She responded with an embrace, continuing her conversation as they went.

Pattinson and Waterhouse made their red carpet debut in Giza, Egypt, while attending the Dior fall 2023 menswear show. As the couple posed for the cameras, they giggled and flirted with one another like they were on their first date.

Later that month, on December 28, the couple was seen making their way through JFK like many holiday travelers. Waterhouse had a few bags over her shoulders, but Pattinson was pushing the majority of their luggage from the trip on a cart, with a guitar slung across his back.

Waterhouse and Pattinson started the new year together. People reported that the two threw a New Year’s Eve party at the Moxy Hotel on New York City’s Lower East Side. A source told the outlet, “Rob and Suki had a great time. He had a table in the corner and was laughing a lot. He and Suki were by each other’s side the entire night. It was a fun evening.”

The Times published an interview with Waterhouse, where she spoke more openly about their relationship than ever before. The outlet revealed they live in London together. “I’m shocked that I’m so happy with someone for nearly five years,” Waterhouse said, noting that they don’t really spend long apart.

On whether they give each other acting advice, she said, “Rob definitely isn’t getting advice from me about acting, but of course I’ll try and get him to help me with an audition before he falls asleep on the sofa.”

Communication makes their relationship work, she added: “I’m always incredibly excited when I see his name pop up [on my phone] or even a text, and I think he feels the same about me,” she said. “We’ve always got so much to say, and I find him hilarious.”

The two both grew up in southwest London and marvel over the fact they ended up together, with such similar journeys in the entertainment industry. “We always say that I never, ever would have thought I’d go out with a boy from Barnes, and he didn’t think he’d go out with a girl from Chiswick,” Waterhouse said.

She didn’t address her future plans with Pattinson explicitly but did say generally she hopes to start a family someday. “You have to be like, ‘I’m going be a sitting cow for a bit of time,’ but it’s going to be worth it,” she said of having children. “I can’t wait. I wish you could click your fingers to make it happen.”

Waterhouse appeared in an interview on CBS Mornings to discuss how she prepared to play keyboardist Karen Sirko in the new Amazon Prime Video series Daisy Jones & The Six. It involved lots of practicing that she said Pattinson had to sit through in their new home.

“Did he enjoy that? Yeah, probably not,” she joked about the practice sessions. But she added that he has his own musical abilities—the actor performed two songs on the Twilight soundtrack, with credits for co-writing “Let Me Sign.”

“He’s actually way worse at being annoying about—well, because he’s an amazing pianist and a really great guitarist,” Waterhouse explained. “He’s amazing, honestly.”

He apparently plays his music for her a lot, and she quipped, “He wins the annoying competition.”

Pattinson and Waterhouse made their Met Gala debut, posing on the red carpet alongside each other:

Waterhouse and Pattinson signaled once more that all is going well between them when they were photographed holding hands while out for a walk in New York City on July 30.

On Saturday, October 21, Waterhouse and Pattinson attended the GO Campaign’s annual gala in Los Angeles. Waterhouse wore a sheer burgundy dress that showed her matching bra and underwear beneath, and Pattinson had on a black suit with a black button-down shirt.

Inside, photos showed them at their table with Waterhouse wearing his blazer over her shoulders. The nonprofit GO raises money for orphans worldwide, and Pattinson is one of their ambassadors.

The pair was photographed on a hike in Los Angeles on November 1. She wore a loose navy sweater with gray shorts, while he was in a gray hoodie and shorts.

Now that the role is his, Pattinson is already focused on the work ahead. “He’s already putting a lot of work into it. He wants to be a great Bond. He knows how much people are going to expect from him,” the source added.

#6799. Pink Hair Is Back and Everyone From SZA to Adéla Are Making a Case for It

Remember when Kylie Jenner was changing her hair color about every other week, Tumblr was overflowing with pastel-haired girlies, and we were all contemplating whether we could pull off pink hair? Well, dust off your 2016 Pinterest boards, bb, because pink hair is officially making a comeback. But this time, it’s not just King Kylie leading the charge. SZA, Adéla, and even Martha Stewart have been putting their own spins on the color, proving that there’s no one way (or age!) to enter your pink hair era. “Since pink is not a natural hair color, you don’t really have to abide by any typical color analysis rules,” says colorist Emily Claire, which means you have free range to do whatever the heck you’d like.

And the range is range-ing. From electric pink to soft rose gold, I promise there’s a rosy hue for you. Personally, I’m loving this return to hair color that’s just fun—and I’m not the only one. “Recently my clients with pink hair have been requesting baby pink and deep berry pink,” says colorist Cara Craig. Plus, Cosmo called out pink as a top fall hair color trend this year. So, whether you’re ready to go full-on Barbie or want to experiment with a subtle rosy tint, there’s a pink hair idea with your name on it. Ahead, we’re breaking it all down, including how to choose your shade, what to ask for at the salon, and how to keep your pink hair looking fresh.

Short answer: Yes. There’s a truly pink hair color for everyone. “I have clients asking for all shades of pink, from blush and rose gold to hot pink to magenta,” says hairstylist Alyssa Chapa.

Pink is surprisingly so versatile, so there are plenty of ways to make it work for you. “In my opinion, pink is a neutral. I think of fashion colors as cousins to classic shades,” says Craig. “So if you are a blonde, consider baby pink. If you are a brunette you’ll want to move to darker pinks and fuchsias. If you want to feel like a redhead then wear rose golds and warm pinks.” She also recommends a violet pink if you prefer keeping things cool-toned.

Wondering about how your skin tone will look with pink hair? “I’m personally of the opinion that there is no right or wrong shade for your skin tone,” says Chapa, but if it’s really important to you, here are her tips for finding the best hair color for your skin tone. “Start by figuring out your undertones,” she says. “I like using the veins on the inside of the wrist; if you have blue or purple veins then you usually have cool undertones, green veins mean warm undertones, and a mixture of both is a neutral undertone.” Then, it’s pretty easy from there: Match your undertones to the shade of pink, which your colorist will be able to help out with (think baby or icy pink for cool tones, peach or salmon pink for warm tones, that kind of thing).

First things first: Bring reference photos to your colorist—we’ve handily included some pics throughout this story for ya. After all, Adéla’s vivid pink and Stewart’s subtle rose gold hair require very different approaches, so you’ll want to make sure you’re specific about what shade you’re after.

“For most people, unless you happen to be naturally blonde, the process would involve lightening your hair to the desired level with bleach, then toning it to the desired pink with a direct dye,” says Claire.

Need some specific pink hair ideas? These are colorist-approved: “One of my favorite ways to wear pink lately is over classic blonde highlights,” says Craig. “I also love a pink double process (e.g. Adéla).” Double process just means a two-step coloring method—your colorist will first bleach/lighten your hair, then apply the pink color. You can also go with chunky highlights, “especially a halo hairline where the pink frames the face,” adds Chapa. “Mixing chunky pink highlights in with shades of red or brown to create a kind of calico effect is also popular online.”

Now for the not-so-fun part: Pink hair doesn’t necessarily equal low-maintenance hair. “No matter the tone, you’re going to have to refresh it in four to six weeks if you want it to stay pink,” says Chapa. If you want to go as low-maintenance as possible, a softer pink is the way to go, notes Craig.

For a more natural-looking grow-out or to keep your hair color easy, “your alternatives are to choose an already muted color like a dusty rose or mauve and let it fade to blonde or brunette, or to invest in an at-home color depositing treatment to maintain your pink until your next salon visit,” Chapa says.

You can help extend your color by washing less frequently, using color-safe shampoo and conditioner, limiting heat styling, and incorporating a color-depositing mask or at-home hair gloss. “I always recommend my clients use a pink-tinted shampoo or conditioner to keep up with the color between appointments at home,” says Claire.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo. She’s covered all things skincare, makeup, hair, and more, including trending haircuts and hair colors you have to try.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan and was previously the beauty assistant at Good Housekeeping, Woman's Day, and Prevention.

#6798. James Bond’s Favorite Luggage Brand Has Broken Its Own Rules

Globe-Trotter has spent more than a century perfecting its signature suitcase. Now it's trying something different.

James Bond has always travelled in style. And while Daniel Craig's 007 was most immediately associated with his Aston Martins, Omega watches, and Tom Ford suits, his luggage of choice was Globe-Trotter, the Hertfordshire-based manufacturer whose cases have also found favor with everyone from Queen Elizabeth II to Kate Moss.

Now the company has done something completely left-field. After 129 years of making essentially the same kind of suitcase, it has changed the formula.

The new GT897 is Globe-Trotter's lightest case yet, and a significant departure from the design that made the brand famous. Out go the traditional rigid frame and locks, replaced by a zip-around opening and softer, more streamlined silhouette.

That said, some familiar details keep it firmly on-brand: the vulcanized fiberboard, leather trim, nickel hardware, and those trademark exposed rivets. And the cases are still handcrafted in Hertfordshire.

Currently available in two color combinations—bland-and-black and green-and-brown—the GT897 is priced at $1,395. A black-and-oxblood version follows in February.

It's an interesting move for a company whose USP has always rested somewhat on its refusal to change. Whether the new James Bond will follow Craig's lead remains to be seen. But at least there's now a new option for packing his tuxedo.

#6795. Zohran Mamdani’s Mustache Is Singlehandedly Bringing Movember Back

When New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani passed out water bottles to marathoners on Nov. 1, few clocked the newly mustachioned man as the city’s head honcho. After all, he’s the first bearded NYC mayor in over a century after, and his constituents had grown familiar with his signature look. When images of his new facial hair circulated, people wondered what inspired the change. Had the mayor been influenced by his hip Brooklyn constituents enough to grow his own on-trend mustache? As we learned the day after the marathon in an online video, the mustache was in support of a somewhat-ancient tradition: Movember.

If it feels like no one’s talked about Movember for a while, that’s because the non-profit charity’s heyday online peaked in 2012. That year, according to the Australian-based foundation, over 1.1 million people participated in Movember—a campaign that encourages men to grow mustaches to raise awareness and funds for men’s mental health, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer—collecting more than $126 million in charity. But like planking, “Gangnam Style,” and flash mobs, Movember eventually faded from the cultural conversation. Google Trends recorded a 10% drop in searches for the cause the following year, and by 2026, search interest had fallen 90% from its 2012 peak. Now, after Mamdani, alongside Council Member Rita Joseph, announced a $4 million investment in a new prostate cancer center at Brooklyn’s Kings County Hospital in honor of the hairy month-long social movement, interest in Movember has since climbed to its highest level since 2019, according to Google Trends.

While the mayor’s stubble has come and gone throughout the month, the heavy mustache has remained constant.

The stubble around the mustache has come and gone during the month, but that thick mustache has remained a staple. He had it at a Veterans Day reception, during a plethora of press conferences, and when he announced the disbanding of the New York Police Department’s controversial Strategic Response Group.

Politicians have long been defined, at least in part, by their hair: Donald Trump’s comb-over, Bernie Sanders’ horseshoe-shaped hairline, Gavin Newsom’s slicked-back locks. But facial hair is increasingly becoming part of the political image, too, as more men embrace letting their beards grow. Pete Buttigieg, once clean-shaven, grew a beard after leaving his post as Transportation Secretary; JD Vance became the first bearded vice president in decades; and Mamdani ended more than a century’s worth of clean-shaven NYC mayors.

And hey, what better time to revive an early 2010s tradition than following the Democrats’ historic victories in the midterm elections. Millennial woke optimism is back, baby, and so is growing facial hair for a charitable cause. If the mayor’s facial hair can turn a bygone internet fad into renewed attention for men’s health, it may be his most consequential grooming decision yet.

#6793. Who Will Be the New Bond Villain? We Nominate These 5 Actors.

Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the new 007, but every Bond needs a worthy adversary.

As Alfred Hitchcock put it: “The better the villain, the better the picture.” And nowhere is this truer than for James Bond—a character whose movie is only as good as its baddie.

Jaws, Blofeld, Le Chiffre, Goldfinger—they are the daddies of all baddies; they put the “fun” in funeral, the “ooh-er” in evildoer. They all have a thing, too, because a good baddie always needs a thing. Jaws has the teeth, Le Chiffre the bleeding eye, Blofeld the needy cat, and Goldfinger, well, he’s a kinky old bastard who paints women head to toe in gold to feel like he’s bonking his own bullion.

Which brings me to the question tugging at every Bond fan’s cufflink. Now that Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the new 007, he’ll need a gold-plated villain to go about “expecting” him.

So which actors would you like to see as the next Bond villain? We have some ideas.

Not famous enough, you say? Not got the chops for such a big-ticket role? Hasn’t earned it, has he? Pah, I’m here to say the actor-slash-musician has already played the best villain on television this year in MobLand’s Frankie Cooper. I’ve gushed about that performance on this website before, and I will again. He plays Cooper with the creeping, glassy-eyed energy of Jimmy Savile—all tracksuits and mirthful threats. But into that he stirs a dollop of Ben Kingsley’s Don “Yes you fucking will” Logan in Sexy Beast. There’s a light nod to Heath Ledger’s Joker there too. In all, it’s a monumental performance—laconically camp, cockney, impishly insane, and properly cackle-out-loud funny. For copyright reasons, I suppose we can’t expect a carbon copy of Frankie transplanted into Bond. But he offers the same vibe: a villain at once unsettling and amusing, which is the hardest trick in the Bond playbook.

There was something in the way he played Pennywise in the adaptation of Stephen King’s It that crawled under my skin like a hookworm. I think it’s the eyes. Bill Skarsgård has a mild lazy eye, which he uses in certain roles to create a disorienting swivel-eyed gaze. He used it for Pennywise. He’s a uniquely physical actor, too, well versed in roles that make children cry. He uses his body like a prop, twisting, deforming, looming, leering as the part demands. He played Count Orlok in Nosferatu, Eric Draven in The Crow and Marquis Vincent Bisset de Gramont in John Wick: Chapter 4. A small snag: he recently said he was “spent” playing bad guys. But he added that, if the right Bond villain landed on his desk, he’d be tempted out of baddie retirement for one last job. “[I] just want to go in and do one Mads Mikkelsen villain,” said the actor, referencing Mikkelsen’s character, Le Chiffre, in Casino Royale.

It’s time for a female lead villain. Sure, Bond has known plenty of miscreant women and seductresses, from Xenia Onatopp (GoldenEye) to Pussy Galore (Goldfinger). But few outright lead villains—hat tip to Lotte Lenya (Rosa Klebb in From Russia with Love) and Sophie Marceau (Elektra King in The World Is Not Enough). It’s a part for a proper actor, a doyenne of screen and stage. A dame, no less. Judi Dench played M across seven films as the one person Bond couldn’t charm, scold, or seduce his way past. Imagine that same withering, headmistress-like authority pointed the other way. Helen Mirren has the gravitas and the twinkle. She’s an Oscar winner who has played a queen, a gangster’s mum in the Fast & Furious films and, of course, the foul-mouthed matriarch Maeve Harrigan in MobLand. She would hardly break a sweat as a Bond villain.

Look at that face: the heavy brow, the gaunt cheeks, the dark, brooding eyes. It’s a face that looks like it was carved by candlelight—a mug made for lurking in the shadows. He’s got a bunch of baddies in his locker, from M. Bison in Street Fighter (2026) to Gareth, the Gemini Killer, in Dexter: Resurrection (2025). But perhaps his biggest ace in the hole is his turn as Piter De Vries in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune (2021). Villeneuve likes to work with actors he knows.

Oh, and the other thing: he really wants it. Dastmalchian explained why in a 2023 interview with /Film: “Trust me when I say that I can bring something to an enemy of 007, whether he or she or they be played in a way that no one has ever seen Bond brought to life before, which is, of course, the way that you guys always do it. I think there’s no one to push Bond to the limits of their capabilities the way that I could, and I would love to do it. So there’s my pitch to them. I can’t wait for them to read this.”

She’s already won an Oscar for playing a corporate villain in Michael Clayton, and she’s never met a prosthetic nose, fur collar or killer blow-dry she couldn’t weaponize... see Snowpiercer’s Minister Mason, Okja’s Lucy Mirando or the White Witch of Narnia—tick, tick, tick. She’s a chameleon with a stare that could freeze a martini.

More than that, Swinton is a master (mistress?) of the in-between, able to embrace and blur lines of gender, age, and species at the click of a slender finger. She possesses that rarest of powers: to change her physical presence, voice, and demeanor so completely as to render herself unrecognizable. Give her a lair, great hair and a long cigarette holder (maybe a Strawberry Ice vape—it’s 2026), and you have a thing of beauty and terror. Because if every great Bond villain needs a thing, Swinton’s is that she can be anything.

#6792. The Launch: November’s Must-Know Fashion News

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fall is in full swing, and with it, so is the fashion industry. As the leaves continue to turn and preparations for the holiday season get serious, brands are finding new ways to celebrate with exciting new capsules, collaborations, and stocking-worthy releases. Look no further than J.J. Martin, whose new book, Table Energy, explores the art of Italian entertaining, and Rimowa x Maison Margiela, which turns travel into something even more desirable. Plus, there’s plenty of reason to get out and shop, with the likes of L/Uniform, Danielle Frankel, and Bulgari all opening new storefronts. Below, all the fashion news to know this month.

Where: Online at gap.com and in select Gap stores

Why: Zac Posen is keeping things simple this winter season—and the latest GapStudio wardrobe is edited to just 12 pieces. The designer’s capsule gives familiar staples a sharper feel through sleek silhouettes, precise tailoring, and touches of unexpected texture like a playful teddy bear coat rendered in a cozy caramel fabric. Other highlights include elevated essentials that Posen has prioritized at the brand: a turtleneck maxi dress, a sleek poplin shirt, and high-rise seamed stirrup jeans. “For winter 2026, we wanted to move beyond traditional occasion wear with versatile pieces designed to be worn from day to night,” Posen said of the collection, which came to life on singer EJAE in the accompanying campaign, in a statement. “There’s still that level of drama with thoughtful tailoring and exaggerated lines, but it’s balanced by a focused palette that feels elegant and wearable.”

Why: Parisian leather goods label L/Uniform is making its New York debut with a flagship on the Upper East Side. Following boutiques in Paris and Tokyo, the store marks the brand’s first American address with founder Jeanne Signoles working with architect Jakob Sprenger to create a space that balances the polish of a boutique with the practical spirit at the heart of the label. “Opening a store in New York was a priority for me from the very beginning,” Signoles says. “I always felt that L/Uniform naturally belonged here, with the city’s energy, its independence, and its very strong connection to everyday life. Our bags are made to be used—to work, to travel, to accompany daily life.”

Why: A historic Tribeca landmark is the setting for Danielle Frankel’s new flagship. At 6 Harrison Street, the bridal house has created a 12,000-square-foot space where original architectural character meets a considered, contemporary interior by Augusta Hoffman Studio. Private rooms make space for a more personal appointment, while the wider setting invites visitors to explore the collection at ease.

Danielle Frankel Chantilly Lace Degradé Border Drop Veil

What: High jewelry collection and new boutique

Why: A 1920s Palm Beach estate is a fitting setting for Bulgari’s first U.S. presentation of “Eclettica.” Designed by Addison Mizner, the waterfront home hosted a gala that also marked the opening of the house’s new boutique. Venus Williams, Chanel Iman, and Becca Bloom were among the guests, with Jewel performing. The collection includes 15 transformable designs—the most Bulgari has presented in a single collection—alongside more than 50 high jewelry pieces. With its Roman roots and sculptural approach to high jewelry, Bulgari’s “Eclettica” brings a distinctly Italian point of view to Palm Beach.

Where: Online at rimowa.com and maisonmargiela.com and select Rimowa and Maison Margiela stores

Why: Some things look better after they’ve been lived in. That idea is at the heart of Rimowa and Maison Margiela’s new travel collaboration, which brings together two signatures: the German luggage house’s familiar grooves and Margiela’s hand-painted white Bianchetto finish. Designed to change with use, the suitcase and matching bag will take on marks and patina as they travel. A campaign by Dexter Lander brings that idea to life in a Haussmannian apartment, where the white paint seems to spill beyond the pieces themselves.

What: Bird on a Rock installation, window displays, and holiday décor

Where: The Landmark; 727 5th Avenue, New York, NY

Why: Tiffany & Co. has switched on the holiday season at The Landmark, with Amanda Seyfried leading the way. The actress lit the flagship’s Bird on a Rock installation by placing an ornament on its Blue Box tree, marking the third year of the display and a full-circle moment. Seyfried stars in the house’s new holiday film, “You & Me,” which travels between present-day New York and a memory from the ’90s. Mikey Madison, Jordyn Woods, and Louisa Jacobson joined the celebration.

Tiffany & Co. Bird on a Rock Wings Narrow Ring

Why: Just in time for the holidays, La DoubleJ founder J.J. Martin has released Table Energy, a new book about the art of Italian entertaining, with a foreword by fashion writer Leandra Medine Cohen. Its pages move from alfresco lunches to candlelit dinners, all in the colorful, convivial spirit of La DoubleJ. The book made its debut at the brand’s Upper East Side boutique, The Lighthouse, where Martin, ELLE Decor’s head of editorial content Elisa Lipsky-Karasz, and ELLE editor-in-chief Nina Garcia gathered to celebrate l’art de la table.

Where: Online at tecovas.com, aninebing.com, and select retail locations

Why: Anine Bing has a new way to kick up a look. The designer has teamed up with Tecovas on a capsule that reworks the label’s Loretta and Jamie boots with star embroidery and polished goat leather. Cowboy hats and belts round out the lineup, which launches alongside Anine Bing’s spring/summer 2027 collection.

#6791. With Grand Theft Auto VI, Rockstar Bet $1.5B That Humans Could Make a Better Game Than AI

Somewhere in the far north of Leonida, Grand Theft Auto VI’s fictional take on Florida, a robbery is taking place. This much is unsurprising. Crime is baked into the title of the series, which began in 1997 and, despite its thick American accent, is still predominantly made in Scotland. But Jason and Lucia, the young, beautiful Bonnie and Clyde who together share the role of protagonists in GTA VI, are not the ones committing this crime. Rather, a grizzled biker hangs from the second-floor window of a locked bar, throwing valuables down to his accomplice on the street.

A thunderstorm has recently rolled through this area and the tarmac steams as sunlight knifes through the clouds. It’s Leonida-muggy. Patches of sweat swell beneath Jason’s arms as he takes in the scene. The bikers notice you watching and ask, politely, considering the circumstances, if you could fuck off. A choice presents itself: clamber back on your stolen motorbike and continue your road trip, or insert yourself into this micro-drama and take a principled stand on behalf of concerned citizens everywhere (then take the loot for yourself, of course).

Dozens of impromptu moments like this stud GTA6, a video game that makes you feel like one entity among many rather than the spoiled V.I.P. around whom everything has been artfully arranged. Most video games flatter the player by making them the centre of the virtual universe, the cog on which all the digital clockwork turns. What is extraordinary about Vice City and its surrounding area is how much of the world appears to trundle on without needing your presence or input.

These moments are made possible by dozens of interlocking systems built by dozens of discrete teams. An entire Los-Angeles-based team worked on the personalities and behaviors of the thousands of people who inhabit Vice City; the bar’s interior was meticulously set-dressed to suggest the lives and tastes of its proprietors and patrons, while the biker’s dialogue and reactions to your choices were written, cast and performed. The weather, too, is restless: cloud and rain move across the world, dynamically changing light and mood. This tableaux, which only a small percentage of players may ever encounter, has not been staged like a scene in a play but rather cultivated in what amounts to the world’s most expensive Petri dish.

Since 1984, when Elite first used procedural generation to conjure an entire galaxy on a computer screen, game designers have learned to produce universes from scant technological resources. But in the era of procedural generation, scale is almost routine; the harder, more costly work is making an expanse feel handmade and coherent. GTA VI manages both, with districts populated by distinct communities and social strata, each shaped by decades of imagined history. It reveals a kind of detail and thoughtfulness that A.I. has yet to reproduce convincingly—and perhaps never will.

The game’s lavishness is not only visible in the rain, the sweat and the individual strands of hair falling across Lucia’s shoulders, but also in the hundreds, perhaps thousands, of diversions away from the criminal grind. For example, Jason and Lucia can take time out from planning a heist to compete in illegal street races for prize money, enter dirt-bike scrambles or race stock cars in a stadium. You can become a hunter, choosing a rifle to suit your quarry so as not to ruin its pelt; start drone racing, streaking through abandoned buildings in an FPV headset; or dive for treasure among old shipwrecks, dodging both the circling sharks, and the authorities who want to check your license.

A compelling main story runs through the game, with missions that leave room for different approaches: you might play as a careful shooter, aiming to wound rather than kill, or as a less discerning one. The couple, so artfully written and performed, offer vivid points of entry into the world as you guide them from relative poverty towards financial security that, perhaps, might allow them to build a family life beyond crime. But much of the joy comes from straying from the main path.

To that end the game makes room for long, meandering drives across the country and peaceful early-morning flights over mountain ranges. You can spend a sleepy afternoon with a scenic view, peering through dollar-a-minute binoculars. Many of these diversions appeared in the studio’s earlier games, but here they feel newly vivid, rendered with extraordinary fidelity. The smaller encounters are just as memorable. Happen upon a possum at night and it might play dead on the tarmac. In a thrift store, you can while away assembling fits worthy of a Ralph Lauren vintage buyer; at a 24-hour nightclub, you can dance until sunrise, before emerging blinking into the dawn while wondering, as Kanye once put it, if they’ve got cabs still. (Of course they do: you can summon one in an instant from your virtual phone).

This is lavish game-making on an unprecedented scale. The irony, however, is that GTA VI arrives at a moment when other studios are bleeding staff (if they survive at all) and the cost of making games at anywhere close to this level continues to rise precipitously. In one industry survey published this month, a third of respondents said they had been laid off in the past two years; more than half of those laid off had yet to find new work—a stark picture of the ongoing insecurity across the industry. In the early 2010s, game budgets fell between $30 and $70 million. McKinsey puts the current cost of a blockbuster game production at $200 million to $500 million. At these prices, few can pay to play.

Even amid the union-busting allegations (which Rockstar denies; an employment tribunal is ongoing), the company has retained much of its long-serving talent between major releases. That continuity gives it a store of institutional knowledge that is hard to preserve when studios expand and contract around individual projects. Key members of GTA VI’s leadership have worked together for decades. The studio also has a clear commercial advantage over its closest creative peers: Naughty Dog, creator of the Uncharted and The Last of Us series, and CD Projekt Red, creator of The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077. Their story-led games can dominate a moment, but their stories conclude when the credits roll.

After players finished Grand Theft Auto V’s story, by contrast, they could continue to inhabit its world through GTA Online, joining others in an ever-replenishing sandbox of play. A leak of Rockstar data suggested that GTA Online averaged about $9.6 million a week between September 2025 and April 2026—roughly $42 million a month. Rockstar is owned by Take-Two, and there is no evidence that GTA Online’s astonishing revenue was entirely funneled into GTA VI. But a game generating revenue year after year gives its parent a durable source of income, justifying artisanal-style work. These factors make Grand Theft Auto VI’s scale and fidelity exceptionally difficult for any rival to match.

That challenge is something even Rockstar’s former leaders have had to reckon with. Leslie Benzies—who for years was one of the three creative leaders on Rockstar projects alongside Sam and Dan Houser (of the trio, only Sam remains at the company)—founded Build a Rocket Boy, which raised more than $300 million before releasing MindsEye. The game’s troubled launch was followed by mass redundancies and, in September 2026, a slide into administration. The lesson seems clear. Money alone cannot buy the infrastructure, expertise and returning audience that have allowed Rockstar to build this world at extraordinary length.

In a game filled with enticing luxuries, from expensive shoes to glinting supercars, the visible human hand is, in this dawning age of AI abundance, the rarest luxury of all in Leonida. You can leave the bikers to their robbery: clouds drift on, the tarmac dries. The world keeps its own time. Making that unforced life cohere took years of work across many teams, and required a collective attention to every detail. With budgets rising and studios closing, perhaps no other company could afford such a wager. Leonida is a miracle of craft—and a monument to a form of game-making the wider industry can no longer sustain.

#6788. Yes, Katie and Victor Were Flirting on ‘The Traitors: New Blood’—and They Dished All About Their First Date

Nothing says romance like trying not to get murdered on reality TV.

The Traitors may be a game of deceit, but Victor Vollbrechthausen and Katie Fites’ flirtation? That was apparently very real.

As the first civilian-only season of The Traitors: New Blood came to a close, host Alan Cumming asked Katie, “Is there a possible date on the cards for you and Victor?”

She seemed tainted by the fact that Victor had banished her, jokingly saying, “No date for you,” until he kept the banter going and claimed that he “earned it” after finding out she was a Traitor. Now, the star-crossed Faithful and Traitor romance has seemingly made its way out of Alan’s Scottish castle.

During a joint postseason interview with Entertainment Weekly, Victor and Katie revealed they followed through on their plans and actually went on a first date.

“We have gone on that date. After incessant begging, let the kids back home know that persistence works,” Katie joked, before revealing that it was “great.”

“It was fun to get to know each other outside of her trying to murder me, me trying not to get murdered. It was nice to take a moment just for us,” Victor, who played as a Faithful while Katie was one of the season’s Traitors, told the outlet.

As for what their first date entailed? Well, there was certainly no discussion about their time on the show, since Victor banned any mention of it. And, honestly, who can blame him? After all, he was onto Katie’s strategy to potentially target him for murder.

While her crush on Victor helped her game, Katie admitted that she genuinely enjoyed hanging out with him and even grew close to him throughout the season. She also revealed that she didn’t immediately kill Victor off because she wasn’t aware of his suspicions toward her—though he had been side-eyeing her earlier on than she realized.

The pair remained coy about whether they’ll keep their showmance going offscreen. When asked if they had plans to go on a second date, Victor shared, “Let’s see. Listen, man, it’s gonna... I don’t know. Getting that first one was an uphill battle, but I think there could be.”

“I think there could be,” Katie added. “But we’ll see. Gonna have to keep persisting.”

#6787. “It Was Never About Fashion”: Emily in Paris’s Costume Designer Reveals the Method to Her Madness

“Emily in Paris: Fashion Without Rules,” a new show at SCAD Fashion in Atlanta, is devoted to the series’s unique style

Emily in Paris premiered when audiences needed it most. The Netflix original, created by Sex and the City producer Darren Star, offered an escapist fantasy: a young girl trying to find love and success in Paris in October 2020. The show functioned as a reprieve from the pandemic, a dreamy alternative in which we could vicariously live through Emily (Lily Collins) as she gallivanted around the City of Light. It was and still is delectably digestible television.

The love for Emily in Paris was anything but unanimous. Critics wasted no time tearing the show apart, with some targeting its depictions of French culture or claiming the script lacked the bite of Star’s previous television shows. The criticism extended to Emily’s idiosyncratic wardrobe, with some writing that the clothing leaned hard on American stereotypes of French fashion or looked cartoonish, with clashing patterns and bright colors. Costume designer Marylin Fitoussi took these criticisms head-on and doubled down. Emily’s outfits weren’t meant to be couture or designer; they were meant to dress a girl finding her sense of self, expressing her desire to explore the unknown.

For six seasons, Fitoussi curated a wardrobe fit for Emily, a bright-eyed young woman unafraid to try something new, to break the rules. This mirrors Fitoussi’s personal philosophy on clothing: that fashion is meant to break rules, to push boundaries, to provide a space of unrelenting experimentation. Ahead of the sixth season, SCAD FASH Museum of Fashion + Film compiles six seasons’ worth of outfits in “Emily in Paris: Fashion Without Rules,” on view through March 14, 2027. The exhibition lives up to its name; for the designer, clothing is a mode of expression that lets anyone feel free, wherever they are. It offers a character study, tracing Emily’s evolution from a doe-eyed expat to a well-versed Parisian resident. (And worry not, there are also looks from Emily’s chic boss Sylvie—played with devastating elegance by Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu.)

Ahead of season 6, Bazaar sat down with Fitoussi at SCAD Fashion in Atlanta to discuss working with Lily Collins, her swan song for Emily in Paris, and how everyone has the potential for creativity.

Marylin Fitoussi: I don’t recall a contemporary TV show being in the spotlight in this way. Generally, when you think of an exhibition, you think of period pieces or couture pieces. The show is really part of pop culture now!

MF: I was surprised when fashion magazines [criticized the show] at the beginning. I’m not a fashion designer, [but] I love fashion and I love clothes. This show was not about fashion at the beginning. [Emily] is a bubbly character with a very strong personality from Chicago; she couldn’t have come dressed in Comme des Garçons or in Yamamoto. I needed to have this cultural shock. She’s a fish-out-of-water character, and we needed something to catch the audience’s eyes. When you want to show people that you love the culture but you can’t express it because you don’t know the codes, you don’t speak the language, the only way you find it is through clothes. It was never about “fashion.” Sometimes, it’s about creativity, individuality, making something not trendy at all. The audience got that, and fashion magazines didn’t get it, so they killed me.

MF: Many times, I’ve asked myself, “Why does this little gingham suit have so much influence?” It’s quite simple. It was the most duplicated, copied, reposted, fan-arted, and used as a Halloween costume. It touched people because it was for them. The French can have their own version of it, their own concept, but for the entire world, it was this one little girly, timeless outfit with the red beret, the red lips, the red soul.

MF: She read the bad press after the release of season 1, and we had a talk. I said they hated it in France; they find it hideous. [I asked her] “Do you want me to change [it]?” She was smiling and said, “No, we can’t, and we won’t please everybody. We need to keep this strong DNA. We need to continue to have this unexpected silhouette because it’s what catches the audience’s eye.” It’s a guilty pleasure. We can say, I love it.

It opens a way for the audience to see fashion in a different way, where you can mix in an awkward way and free people from this law where you shouldn’t [do that]. Coco Chanel used to say, “Before leaving a room, look at yourself in the mirror and take something out.” I always say, “Put something more on.”

MF: I wanted to present a more elevated version, more mature, more evolved, but still true to what she was and what she is, with an eclectic combination and a little bit awkward. She knows the French rules, but as I do, she finds French fashion so boring. In general, I find that fashion is less and less interesting. Why are fashion and celebrity stylists sourcing more and more from archives? What it’s showing is that now everything is the same. Everything is boring, and I understand why. They need to sell the show! We don’t have to sell anything. We have to sell dreams, illusions, craziness, boldness. People watch the show in groups. Some people say, “I love it,” and some say, “I hate it,” and they have a dialogue and fight and have a good [time]. We love that.

MF: A young designer wants to be famous right away. Fame doesn’t happen, and it doesn’t matter. You need to be happy with what you’re doing. With costume design versus fashion design, you can be much freer. You don’t have anything to sell, and you don’t have to design the “It bag.” If your show is successful, it’s a win-win for everybody. To see that, you need to be true to your vision. You need to be true to your gut feeling, to your vision, to your DNA. Talent is not enough; you need to be at the right place at the right time. Being discovered by Darren Star … he changed my life. At some point, you find the right project for you.

You need to work a lot to take care of every detail. You need to be strong and push the boundaries. You need to try to show a different way to see costumes and clothes, to see that everything is possible…. Style begins when fear ends. You don’t want to please everybody, and I’m always attracted to people who dress in a different way, and I’m never judgmental. To create something is to expose yourself. It’s very vulnerable. It’s brave.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6786. Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Are Married

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have officially tied the knot. Entertainment Tonight reported that they got married in Palm Springs on November 21.

Few details about their wedding have emerged, which isn’t surprising given that the couple kept most of the planning private. In March 2026, a source told People that they weren’t interested in having a big wedding—instead, they were envisioning a “smaller and meaningful” celebration.

Cyrus had “ideas” about what she’d like, “but she’s not planning some huge, traditional event,” the source added. “Maxx is extremely private, and that’s just not who he is. When they do get married, it will be something smaller and meaningful to them. Not a big Hollywood production.”

The Bass Persuades singer announced her engagement in December 2025, unveiling the bombé cushion-cut diamond ring Morando gave her at the Avatar: Fire and Ash premiere as she posed with him.

In July, Morando spoke to Wonderland about how he first met Cyrus in 2021. “Sam in my band [Liily], his sister’s friend knew Miley,” he said. “They just put us on a blind date. Which, from Miley’s perspective, I don’t think is really possible, because she’s so in the public eye. So it felt like if there was a way to have a blind date for her, this might be the most blind date that she could do.”

They connected during the date and “just never stopped hanging out,” he said.

It took Morando some time to adjust to the attention Cyrus receives. “When I first met her, that part of it was strange,” he said. “I’ve never experienced people waiting outside places for you and things like that. But as time’s gone on, now it’s kind of the inverse. Whenever we go to some event, that’s when I am reminded that she is who she is, you know. But I love going with her to certain things to support whatever she’s doing.”
